Quick Start

Abbreviations used on this page (TSDB, WAL, TTL, HWM, XPUB, ZMQ, SQLite, JSON, CLI, API, RSS, fd, PEP, CORS, OBS...) are defined in the Abbreviations & jargon section.

You can have sqtseries recording data within a few minutes. You will need Python 3.14 or newer on your computer. The steps below use the bundled Python client; if you prefer other languages or plain web requests, the same steps are shown with HTTP and each language is covered in Client Libraries.

1. Install

pip install sqtseries
Python 3.14+ is required. Using a virtual environment is recommended if you manage multiple Python projects.

2. Start the service

sqtseries run

The service prints its log to the terminal and stays in the foreground (press Ctrl+C to stop it; the shutdown is graceful and exits cleanly). On the first run it creates its database file at ~/.sqtseries/data/db.sqlite and starts background tasks that keep the data tidy.

To choose your own ports and database file, write a config file and pass it with --config. Global flags such as --config and --db belong before the subcommand, not after:

# config.toml — pick your own ports and DB location
[database]
path = "/data/tsdb.sqlite"

[ingestion]
port = 14001

[query]
port = 14002

[streaming]
port = 14003

[admin]
port = 14004

[http]
port = 14005

[stats]
port = 14006

[ports]
auto_detect = false

sqtseries --config config.toml run
python3 -m sqtseries --config config.toml run   # identical
sqtseries --config config.toml status           # status uses the same config
Flag order matters. sqtseries run --config config.toml errors with "No such option" — put global flags (--version, --config, --db, --help) before the subcommand: sqtseries --config config.toml run.

You can also pick just the database on the command line — it overrides both the config file and environment variables:

sqtseries --db /data/tsdb.sqlite run
sqtseries --config prod.toml --db /data/other.sqlite status

If other databases live in the same directory, run prints them so you can pick one with --db; see Configuration for how --db and conflicting databases are handled.

3. Send data

A "measurement" has three parts: a name, a number, and optionally labels (tags). The time is taken from the server clock unless you provide it. Send a few in Python with the bundled client:

from sqtseries import Client

c = Client()
c.write("cpu.usage", 0.72, {"host": "web1", "env": "prod"})
c.write("cpu.usage", 0.65, {"host": "web2", "env": "prod"})
c.write_many([
    {"metric": "mem.usage", "value": 512.0, "tags": {"host": "web1"}},
    {"metric": "mem.usage", "value": 388.0, "tags": {"host": "web2"}},
])

Or over HTTP with the widely available curl tool:

curl -X POST http://127.0.0.1:12505/api/v1/write \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"metric":"cpu.usage","tags":{"host":"web1"},"value":0.72}'

4. Read data back

A query asks for a name, a start and end time, and often an aggregation (such as "average" or "maximum"). The client takes start/end in nanoseconds (epoch); the HTTP gateway takes them in seconds — the Queries page explains this in detail.

from sqtseries import Client
import time

c = Client()
now_ns = time.time_ns()
rows = c.query("cpu.usage", start=now_ns - 3600 * 10**9, end=now_ns)
print(rows)  # e.g. [{'timestamp': 1.7e9, 'value': 0.72}, ...]  # seconds

# Summary numbers for the whole window
stats = c.aggregate("cpu.usage", funcs=["avg", "min", "max", "count", "p95"])
print(stats)

The same over HTTP:

curl "http://127.0.0.1:12505/api/v1/read?metric=cpu.usage&aggregation=avg&interval=1m"
curl "http://127.0.0.1:12505/api/v1/aggregate?metric=cpu.usage&funcs=avg,max,p95"

5. Watch data live

If your data is still arriving, you can watch it as it comes in. Each payload is a measurement that was just accepted.

from sqtseries import Client

c = Client()
for payload in c.subscribe("cpu."):   # prefix match on the metric name
    if payload is not None:            # None = idle heartbeat
        print(payload)                 # e.g. {'metric': 'cpu.usage', 'tags': ..., 'value': ...}

It is also possible from a browser (WebSocket):

const ws = new WebSocket("ws://127.0.0.1:12505/ws/subscribe?metric=cpu.");
ws.onmessage = (e) => console.log(JSON.parse(e.data));

6. Check whether it is healthy

sqtseries status    # pid, version, database path, ports
sqtseries health    # "ok" when the database file is intact
sqtseries ports     # which ports are actually bound
$ sqtseries --config config.toml status
Service: running (pid 2301)
Version:  0.1.0
DB:       /data/tsdb.sqlite
  ingest: 14001
  query: 14002
  stream: 14003
  admin: 14004
  http: 14005
  stats: 14006

$ sqtseries --config config.toml ports
ingest: 14001
query: 14002
stream: 14003
admin: 14004
http: 14005
stats: 14006

health runs a read-only database integrity probe (PRAGMA quick_check) and exits 0 when the answer is ok, 1 when it is degraded. That makes it usable in scripts and service monitors.

7. Run it as a background service

The install command sets up a systemd service that starts sqtseries when your computer boots and keeps it running (a per-user unit by default; install --system targets the system). Pass the same --config you used for run and it is baked into the unit, so your ports and settings survive in the service too:

sqtseries --config config.toml install
sqtseries --config config.toml status
journalctl --user -u sqtseries -f    # follow its logs

Details, including uninstalling, are on the Systemd page.

8. Stop the service

sqtseries --config config.toml stop   # SIGTERM to the running instance

Stopping in the foreground with Ctrl+C does the same graceful shutdown, so data is never left half-written. stop resolves the runtime file next to the database; without a matching --config/--db it refuses to touch an instance serving a different database.

Config file formats

Config files may be .toml, .yaml, or .json. TOML and JSON work with no extra packages; YAML needs pyyaml installed, which is not a dependency of sqtseries — so avoid YAML unless you have (or add) pyyaml separately. A config file can also be selected with the environment variable SQT_SERIES_CONFIG_FILE instead of --config.
